newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa mutineers disarm civilian militias.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa mutineers disarm civilian militias.

text.p: Rebel soldiers in Central African Republic have been searching houses in the capital Bangui in a drive to disarm a civilian militia loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse, rebel officers said on Monday.
French troops, patrolling the city since soldiers revolted on Saturday, did not intervene to stop the searches, residents and rebels said.
The issue of the civilian militia and armed thugs called "Codos" was a cause of previous army mutinies in April and May along with pay and status of the army.

"The disarmament drive which started on Saturday is going well," rebel spokesman Sergeant Roger Kongbossomo told Reuters. "We have at least 500 men on the ground and we will disarm the militia and Codos and give an account of it to the people."
Patasse, who survived a more serious mutiny in May with the help of French troops, is on an official visit to Europe and the date of his return has not been announced.
His prime minister, Jean-Paul Ngoumpande, strongly favours disarmament, which he termed a national priority when he took office as part of concessions offered by Patasse to defuse the May revolt.
Bangui was calm on Monday but several districts were tense because of the disarmament drive by the mutineers.
The army appears divided, with hardline elements mainly from the south refusing to return to barracks. Patasse is backed largely by soldiers from the north, his home region.
Rebels were still in control of national radio's short-wave and medium-wave transmitter south of the capital after seizing it on Sunday. Broadcasts can only be heard on FM.
Shops and businesses opened cautiously on Monday, with French troops and presidential guard units searching cars at several check points.

France has an important military base in Central African Republic, one of the world's poorest countries, under a defence accord, as with many of its former African colonies. Patasse, a civilian, invoked the accord in May to secure French help.

French and loyalist troops guarded the city centre, the presidential palace and Patasse's stronghold districts of Fou, Gonbongo, Boy-Rabe as well as main roads leading to the north and east of the country.
Rebels control the main Kassai barracks, the districts of Kilometre Five, Fatima, Brussels and Petevo as well as the highway leading south and Bangui's main petrol depot.

State radio said mutineers had freed two allies of Patasse seized at the start of the revolt: the general secretary of Patasse's ruling Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People, Joseph Vermond Tchendo, and national police chief Ernest Latakpi.
They were released on Sunday night following an appeal for calm by Interior Minister Jean Willybiro-Sako, it said.
On Monday eight opposition parties and five main labour unions appealed for calm and dialogue, while at the same time denouncing Patasse's "tribalist policies and mismanagement".
The unions, accused by Patasse of fomenting previous unrest, said in their statement they had nothing to do with the mutiny.

Some mutineers said on Saturday they would continue their protest until Patasse returned home. The president attended the World Food Summit in Rome and was due to go on for a five-day official visit to France, aides said.
